concept.name: Commercial trader
concept.definition: In the CFTC's legacy Commitments of Traders report, a reportable trader whose futures positions are commercially motivated — traditionally producers, merchants, processors, and users of the physical commodity who manage business risks by hedging, plus swap dealers offsetting OTC risk in the futures market. In the Disaggregated COT this group is split into Producer/Merchant/Processor/User and Swap Dealers.
concept.intuition: Commercials are the industry players using futures to insure their real business, not to bet on price direction.
concept.mechanics: Classification is made by CFTC staff from Form 40 disclosures and other information, based on the trader's predominant activity; staff classify traders, not individual trades, so a commercial's positions may include some non-hedge activity. Legacy commercial open interest is published long, short, and (for count purposes) spreading.
concept.failure_modes: Because classification follows the trader rather than the trade, commercial positions can include speculation and swap-dealer inventory, muddying the 'hedging' interpretation. Multi-functional organizations are placed in one category by predominant activity, so mixed businesses are imperfectly represented.
concept.misconceptions: Commercials are not automatically 'smart money' that is always right — they are hedgers whose net short in a bull market simply reflects offsetting long physical exposure. Their net position is a byproduct of risk transfer, not a directional forecast.
concept.example: A grain elevator that has bought farmers' corn sells corn futures to lock in the price; in the legacy COT its short futures are reported as commercial positions.

citations.source: CFTC: Disaggregated Commitments of Traders - Explanatory Notes
citations.section: Comparison of the Disaggregated COT Report to the Legacy COT Report
